nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Phylum: Chordata
      Class:  Osteichthyes
      Order:  Perciformes
      Family:  Sparidae
Synonyms: Sparus (Schopf 1788)
 	Sparus probatocephalus (Walbaum 1792)
 	Sparus ovicephalus (Bloch and Schneider 1801)
 	Sargus ovis (Mitchill 1814) (Cuvier and Valenciennes 1830) (Gunther 1859)
 	Diplodus probatocephalus (Jordan and Gilbert 1882)
 	Sargo raiado

 Synonymy for Archosargus aries (Culvier and Valenciennes):
 	Archosargus aries (Jordan and Fesler 1893)
 	Archosargus probatocephalus aries (Eigenmann and Hughes 1887)
 	Sargus aries (Cuvier and Valenciennes 1830) (Gunther 1864)

Common Name: Sheepshead
Other Common Names:  English:  Sheepshead bream, sheepshead porgie (358), convict fish (358 664), striped bandit (1992), and striper (664).  French:  Rondeau mouton (791), tete de mouton (Louisiana French) (1992).  Spanish:  Sargo chopa (791).  California sheepsheads, Pimelometopon pulchrum, are completely different fish species despite the shared common name (956, 1976).

Key Characteristics:  Largest of the Porgies (up to 91 cm and 9 kg) with deep and compressed body.  Large eyes and small mouth; a great distance apart.  Dorsal fins are continuous and caudal fin is deeply forked.  Scales ctenoid.  Front teeth are caninelike and rear teeth are molariform, including those in the pharyngeal mill. The adductor mandibulae (jaws) complex characteristic of many Sparidae fish is described by Hernandez (1987).  The oral jaw musculature is a primary functional determinant of sheepshead feeding ecology (1987).  No barbels on the lower jaw.  Sides are silvery to yellowish and back is darker olive brown, with a broad black bar across nape.  Populations from the western Gulf of Mexico typically have 5 dark bands on body; populations elsewhere have 6; those from Central America and South America have narrower bands (788).  Ginsburg first noted the number of dark bands as the only distinguishing characteristic between the three sheepshead subspecies (1062).  This counting does not include the incomplete bar on the head.  Fins that are in stable positions for all subspecies of sheepshead include the incomplete bar on the head, the two bars positioned below the origin and end of the dorsal fin, and the bar near the base of the caudal fin (1962 1963).

Similar Species:  Three subspecies of sheepshead exist along the western Atlantic seaboard.  A. p. probatocephalus is the northern form ranging from Nova Scotia to Cedar Key, Florida, with no break at the tip of the Florida peninsula (92 791).  A. p. oviceps is likely limited to the northwestern Gulf of Mexico ranging from St. Marks, Florida to Campeche Bank, Mexico (92). A. p. aries is the southern subspecies having narrower bands; ranging from Belize, British Honduras, to Bahia de Sepetiba, just south of Rio de Janeiro, Brazil (92 327 788 791 1962). Caldwell determined A. p. probatocephalus and A. p. oviceps occupy the east and west regions of the Gulf of Mexico, respectively, according to a change in bottom type in the northeastern region of the Gulf (92).  A. p. probatocephalus is prevalent in hard bottom habitat of the eastern Gulf, while A. p. oviceps is common in the northwestern, soft (muddy) bottomed Gulf, east to Alligator Harbor, Florida (92 791).  Ginsburg considered A. p. oviceps as a separate species in part because he observed a majority of his specimens of the 5 banded and variant fish were limited (<74 mm) in size (1062).  A variant is defined for a specimen of A. p. probatocephalus as a non 6-6 bar pattern and for a specimen of A. p. oviceps as a non 5-5 bar pattern (92 1962).  Caldwell, however, documented numerous variants of A. p oviceps within its range (off Destin, Florida) larger than Ginsburg observed (350mm) and apparently from the same local population (1963).  Caldwell maintains that A. p. probatocephalus and A. p. oviceps are only subspecies based on Ginsburg’s historically accepted species classification (92 1989).  Both specimens had typical bar counts less than the required 90% divergence (87%) (92 1989).  Despite these historical findings, current genetic research does not support sheepshead subspecies designations (1980).  Two distinct sheepshead lineages have been identified across the habitat range (1980).  Stock assessments of sheepshead have been completed separately for the Atlantic and Gulf of Mexico waters (1980).

Other: References for Scientific Name include (Walbaum 1792) (Jordan and Fesler 1893) (Gill 1873).  The synonymy is from Jordan and Evermann (1896) and Jordan et al. (1930). Additional synonymy is included for the southern subspecies of sheepshead, Archosargus aries (Cuvier and Valenciennes).

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial:  Sheepshead has some commercial value for food, but its acceptance as a food fish varies among coastal states (358).  They are taken commercially by shrimp trawlers while seining offshore, but are also caught during their spawning season (March to May) when they are most abundant (47).  Average 1958-1960 annual, commercial landings in the Gulf of Mexico were 378,000 lbs. (1978).  During the same time period, 107,200 lbs. of sheepsheads were landed in West Florida and of this total; 23,900 lbs. were landed in Pinellas, Hillsborough, and Manatee counties (1978).  Florida landings data for 1988 indicate that a total of 678,986 pounds worth $206,236 were landed statewide (902).  The total number of pounds landed was greater for the West Coast, but on the East Coast, more fish were landed per trip.  Statewide, 1988 landings averaged 24 fish per trip (902).  They have a low retail value, averaging 46¢ per pound in 1987 and 30¢ per pound in 1988 (902), and incidental trawl catches are probably discarded.  Annual commercial landings averaged 400,000 lbs. statewide before 1986 and gradually increased to over 1,000,000 lbs. in 1992 (1979).
	Statewide commercial sheepshead landings averaged 761,000 lbs. during 1986-1994 and decreased to 284,000 lbs. in 1996 (1980).  This drastic decline (63%) was probably due to the implementation of the net-ban constitutional amendment of July, 1995.  This amendment banned the use of the popular and more effective gill nets and trammel nets.  In 1996, the Atlantic and Gulf coast commercial landings using cast nets increased at least 400% compared to 1992-1994 landings (1980).  The number of Saltwater Product License holders that landed sheepshead also declined 45% from about 2,800 to 1,554 between 1992-1994 and 1996, most likely due to the shift in fishing gear from gill nets to cast nets (1979 1980).  Despite this decrease in Saltwater Product Licenses, the majority (60%) of these license holders landed less than 100 lbs. of sheepshead a year and only 8% landed 1,000 lbs. or more a year (1979).  Commercial landings in Florida during 1996 were greatest in the central coastal counties of the state.  The Atlantic coast counties from St. Johns south to Martin county, accounted for most of the 1996 landings while the Gulf coast landings occurred from Pinellas county south to Lee county (1980).  Murphy and MacDonald noted commercial landings during 1986-1994 averaged 328,000 and 486,000 lbs for the Atlantic and Gulf coasts, then dropped to 144,000 and 166,000 lbs for the Atlantic and Gulf coasts, respectively (2006). In 1996, Murphy (1980) noted that the Atlantic and Gulf coast commercial landings using cast nets increased at least 400% compared with 1992-1994 landings (1980).
	The number of Saltwater Product License holders that landed sheepshead also declined 45% from about 2,800 to 1,554 between 1992-1994 and 1996, most likely due to the shift in fishing gear(s) from gill and trammel nets to cast nets (1979, 1980). Murphy and MacDonald observed that these entangling nets (gill nets and trammel nets) accounted for only 0-20% of the post-1996 commercial landings for both Florida coasts (2006). However, during 1993-1994 these entangling nets comprised 55% and 81% of the commercial landings on the Atlantic and Gulf coasts, respectively (2006).
	In contrast, cast nets and hook-and-line accounted for an annual average of 90% of the 1006-1999 annual landings on the Atlantic coast and 85% of the landings on the Gulf coast (2006). Despite this decrease in Saltwater product Licenses, the majority (60%) of these license holders landed less than 100 lbs of sheepshead a year and  only 8% landed 1,000 lbs or more a year (1979).
	Commercial landings in Florida during 1996, 1997, and 1999 were greatest in the central coastal counties of the state (2007, 2008, 2006). The Atlantic coast counties from St. Johns south of Martin county accounted for most of the 1996 landings while the Gulf coast landings occurred from Pinellas county south of St. Lucie accounted for most of the sheepshead landed on the Atlantic coast. On the Gulf coast, the counties surrounding Tampa Bay and Charlotte Harbor contributed most to the 1999 commercial landings (2006).
	During 2007, commercial landings were greatest from Martin to Volusia Counties and in Duval County, especially in Martin County on the Atlantic coast, and in Lee, Charlotte, Hillsborough, Pinellas, and Escambia Counties on the gulf coast [figref](Fig. 1a). [/figref]
[fig]

[/fig]
[caption]Figure 1a.  Geographic distribution of pounds of sheepshead landed in the commercial fishery during 2007 by region. [/caption]

	The fishing effort (number of trips landing sheepshead) increased through 1992 on the Florida Atlantic coast and increased through 1993 on the Florida Gulf coast.  Effort has dropped on both coasts since then, especially on the Gulf coast where effort dropped from over 25,000 trips in 1993 to less than 10,000 trips in 1996 (1980).  Fishing effort is highly correlated to commercial landings of sheepshead and a decreased level of effort and subsequently landings since 1995 was evident (2006).
	The median size of sheepshead landed has increased on both coasts from 1992-1995.  The median size landed on the Atlantic coast increased from 250 mm FL to almost 300 mm FL while the Gulf coast median size increased from 235-280 mm FL to 300-345 mm FL (1980).  Most sheepshead landed by commercial fishermen in Florida before 1996 were 7-14 inches long yet due to the implementation of the net ban and minimum size limit that has changed.  Since the 1995 regulations, most sheepshead landed have been 11-16 inches (FL) on the Atlantic coast and 12-18 inches (FL) on the Gulf coast (2006).

Recreational:  Florida supports a moderate sport fishery in most months with the greatest catches in between November and April (1980).  It is a common fish in inshore waters, often-caught on fiddler crabs or barnacle bait (327).  Fishery information for the Gulf of Mexico showed a total catch of 3,553,000 sheepshead in 1988 (513).  Sheepshead are frequently discarded because spines make cleaning difficult.  The recreational landings in Florida between 1986-1996 varied for each coast.  The landings on the Atlantic coast ranged from 0.3 million fish (0.6 million lbs.) in 1989 to 1.2 million fish (2.2 million lbs.) in 1994 (1980).  Gulf coast landings ranged from 0.5 million fish (0.9 million lbs.) in 1986 to 2.1 million fish (3.2 million lbs.) in 1992 (1980).  The numbers of sheepshead landed during 1997-1999 decreased on both coasts compared with the early 1990’s. On the Atlantic coast fewer than 374,000 sheepshead were landed recreationally, while on the Gulf coast less than 890,000 sheepshead were landed (2006).
	Most sheepshead landed by anglers in Florida during 1980-1991 ranged from 200 to 450 mm TL and the modal size for both coasts was 300 mm (1979).  The median size sampled from the recreational fishery increased, as in the commercial fishery, from the 1986-1995 period to 1996.  On the Atlantic coast the median size increased from 300 mm FL to 345 mm FL while on the Gulf coast the median size increased from 300 mm FL to 344 mm FL (1980).
	Lengths of most sheepshead landed by recreational fishermen in 1999 were 10-16 inches (FL) on the Atlantic coast and 10-18 inches (FL) on the Gulf coast (Murphy and MacDonald, 2000).  The highest recreational landings in 1996 was more than 100,000 sheepshead for the north and central regions of the Atlantic coast south to Martin county, and from the south and east of Franklin county on the Gulf coast (1980).  In general, higher effort during 1986-1999 resulted in higher total catch.  During the 1986-1999 time frame, the highest catch and effort was seen during 1994 on the Atlantic coast and during 1992 and 1993 on the Gulf coast (2006).
	During 2007, recreational landings were high and evenly distributed in all coastal regions of Florida, with the exception of Monroe County[figref] (Fig. 1b) [/figref].
[fig]

[/fig]
[caption]Figure 1b.  Geographic distribution of numbers of sheepshead landed during 2007 in the recreational fishery by region. [/caption]

	The recreational fishery contributes the majority of the landings to the Florida combined recreational and commercial fishery.  The combined Florida sheepshead landings averaged about 4 million lbs. during 1986-1996 (1980) and in 1999 the total number of sheepshead landed commercially was approximately 1.35 million (2006).  The Gulf coast combined fishery landings averaged 2.4 million lbs. during 1986-1996 while the Atlantic coast averaged 1.6 million lbs. (1980).  In 1996, the recreational fishery made 92% of the combined fishery Gulf coast landings and 86% of the combined fishery Atlantic coast landings (1980).  These percentages increased slightly in 1999 from 86% to 89% on the Gulf coast and from 92% to 96% on the Atlantic coast (2006).

nodes.title: Combined Fisheries
nodes.body:
The estimated annual numbers of sheepshead landed in the total combined fishery have decreased since 1996 compared to previous years (2006). The combined sheepshead landings on the Atlantic coast dropped to an average of 432,000 fish and to approximately 773,000 fish on the Gulf coast since 1996 (2006).
	Florida landings of sheepshead were 2,786,278 pounds in 2007, out of which the recreational fishery made about 90%. Statewide landings in 2005 were greatest on the gulf coast (about 66%) (Mud).
	The 2007 total landings of sheepshead were 3% lower than the average landings in the previous five years (2002–2006) and were 19% lower than the 1982–2007 historical average landings (Fig.2). On the Atlantic coast, total annual landings generally increased between 1989 and 1994 to 2.6 million pounds, decreased to 0.84 million pounds in 1998, increased to 1.3 million pounds in 2005, and decreased to about a million pounds in 2006-2007 (Fig. 2). Gulf coast landings have fluctuated with a peak in 1992, followed by a general decline to 1.6 million pounds through 1997, and have averaged 1.9 million pounds each year since then (Fig. 2).
[fig]

[/fig]
Ecological Role:  Sheepshead predation may be important in controlling the structure of sessile invertebrate and motile epifauna communities (634).

Status:  Need information.

Stock Status:  The fishery management actions implemented for sheepshead in Florida during the mid-1990’s including the ban on the use of entangling nets, the 12-inch minimum size limit, a 15-fish bag limit, and 50 fish commercial possession limit have led to a drop in total landings of sheepshead and a change in the size of fish landed.  Sheepshead spawning stock in Florida has steadily increased and precludes the likelihood of recruitment failure for either the Atlantic or Gulf coast stocks (2006).

Species Stress:  Need information.

nodes.title: STOCK ENHANCEMENT
nodes.body:
Induced Breeding:  Sheepshead may be a viable aquaculture candidate for both the aquarium trade and commercial culture for food (1956. 1954).  Tucker and Barbera injected human chorionic gonadotropin (HCG) into multiple female sheepsheads to induce ovulation and voluntary tank spawning (1954).  Tucker and Barbera have developed HCG injection procedures and determined that female oocytes should be vitellogenic and near 0.4 mm in diameter before attempting HCG hormone injections.

Rearing:  Tucker reared sheepshead from egg to an average 573 g in 13 months.  Sheepshead have high potential for culture due to their tolerance to extreme conditions. Sheepshead require saltwater for only the first 2-5 weeks of rearing although overall survival and daily growth rates were significantly better in saltwater than freshwater (1956). Sheepshead can be reared in pools or pens and have survival and growth rates similar to red sea bream (1956).

Feeding:  Essential feed for sheepshead includes rotifers, artemia nauplii, and salmon starter. After 50 days growth, sheepshead will consume standard salmon commercial feed (1956).  Ogburn notes algae may be an important source of nutrients for juvenile and adult sheepshead and this may be a possible food item for reared sheepshead (1951).

Stocking:  Need information.

Disease Control:  Need information.

nodes.title: POPULATION
nodes.body:
Total Mortality:  Murphy reported a Chapman-Robson pooled estimate of total mortality for sheepshead with fishing mortality being twice the level of natural mortality (1980).  Using Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, Florida Marine Research Institute (FWC, FMRI) data from sheepshead collected with multiple gears on both coasts from 1993-1997 and an age composition dominated by age 2 and age 3 fish, the total annual mortality was 45% or Z = 0.60 (1980).  Muller and Murphy using a catch curve to estimate total mortality obtained similar results.  The Atlantic coast total mortality was 0.49 per year and the Gulf coast total mortality was 0.54 (1979).

Natural Mortality:  No direct measure of natural mortality of sheepshead exists although numerous estimation procedures are available (2003).  Schexnayder estimated natural mortality of sheepshead in Louisiana (1991) using the following authors’ estimation procedures:

      Pauly (1980)					0.40
      Alagaraja (1984)				0.20 and 0.35
      Hoeing (1983)					0.20
      Rikhter and Efanov (1976)			0.77

Fishing Mortality: When using an instantaneous natural mortality of 0.2 per year, Murphy estimated the instantaneous fishing mortality would be 0.40 per year (1980).  These authors also estimated age and year specific fishing mortalities on the Atlantic and Gulf coasts of Florida finding close trends with landings.  The mean instantaneous fishing mortality for age group 3 through 7 averaged 0.53 per year on the Atlantic coast and 0.33 on the Gulf coast (1980).
	Murphy and MacDonald estimated the instantaneous fishing mortality coefficient for the most vulnerable age class of sheepshead for both coasts of Florida (2006).  On the Atlantic coast, the total fishing mortality peaked in 1994 at approximately 0.47 and dropped to between 0.13 and 0.17 during 1997-1999.  Gulf coast fishing mortality for the most vulnerable age group peaked near 0.60 in 1992 then dropped to between 0.17 and 0.21 during 1996-1999 (Figure 7).
	Growth parameters, sexual maturity information, and age-specific selectivities are incorporated into yield per recruit and spawning potential analyses.  These analyses estimate the impact of natural and fishing mortality on yield and spawning potential of the stock (1991).  Schexnayder used catch at age data from the Louisiana recreational and commercial fishery in 1995 and the Sparre and Venema method (2003) to derive age-specific selectivities for use in a yield per recruit analysis (1991).  The selectivities are:
Age 0 = 0
Age 1 = 0.0011
Age 2 = 0.0271
Age 3 = 0.3785
Ages 4 and older = 1
(1991).

	Murphy used a separable population model developed by Patterson and Melvin to estimate age-specific selectivities for Florida sheepshead for the period 1990-1994 (1980).  The reference age used that was most vulnerable to fishing was age 5 (1980). Given data from FMRI’s Fisheries Independent Monitoring program indicate sheepshead become less vulnerable to fishing as they age, the selectivity of age 9 sheepshead was set at 60% of the selectivity for age 5 (1980).  The vulnerability of sheepshead shifted towards older ages between time periods 1986-1995 and 1996-1999 (2006).  Between these time periods and for both the recreational and commercial fisheries on the Atlantic coast, the most vulnerable age shifted from age 4 to age 5, and on the Gulf coast from age 4 to age 6 (Figure 8).  Selectivity was assumed constant after age 7 for the stock assessment conducted during 2000 (2006).

nodes.title: Spawning Potential Ratios
nodes.body:
The spawning biomass of females is assumed to be the factor limiting the spawning potential of sheepshead yet the data available on the maturity of females are unclear (1954, 1958, 1972, 1980, 1981).  This information is critical to completing sheepshead stock assessments (1979).  The yield per recruit and spawning potential analyses for Louisiana sheepshead indicate the fishery prior to existing regulations was operating at F0.1 and well below FMAX, using a conservative M = 0.2, with yield of 76% to 86% of maximum and a spawning potential ratio (SPR) at 40% to 50% (1991).  When M = 0.3, the yield declines from 47% to 66% of maximum and the SPR is 58% to 71% (1991).
	Muller and Murphy calculated SPR’s for Florida sheepshead according to the following ages of female maturity given a conservative natural mortality of 0.15 per year and a fishing mortality of 0.35 per year (1979) as Age 1 (35%), age 2 (29%), age 3 (21%) (1979). The authors calculated spawning potential ratios for these ages because of the uncertainty in female maturity data (1979).  Muller and Murphy concluded the spawning potential ratio for Florida sheepshead is approximately 30% (1979).  Another conclusion from their recruitment analysis was that the years 1991 and 1992 are weaker year classes with sheepshead partially recruiting to the fishery at age 1.  This may result in possible declines in availability and landings (1979).  Murphy generated equilibrium yield per recruit curves for sheepshead using 1996 selectivity patterns and fishing mortalities for each coast, and concluded that sheepshead is insensitive to growth overfishing (1980).  The authors estimated transitional spawning potential ratios for 1996 to be 19% for the Atlantic coast and 28% for the Gulf coast (1980).  Assuming the 1996 fishing levels continue, Murphy expects the spawning potential ratios to increase to 24% on the Atlantic coast and 63% on the Gulf coast (1980).  Estimates for 1999 transitional spawning potential ratios increased as expected to 47% on the Atlantic coast and 49% on the Gulf coast (2006).  With continued 1999 fishing levels, these ratios would likely increase to 60% on the Atlantic coast and 53% on the Gulf coast (2006).
	Assessments of sheepshead in Florida indicate that they were fished near their maximum yield-per recruit in 1994, but fishing mortality has since declined in response to several management initiatives (1979; 1980; 2006; Munyandorero et al. 2006). In response to the drop in fishing mortality, the transitional spawning potential ratios on both coasts have risen steadily since 1996. The estimated transitional SPR has increased from 40% in 1995 to above 60% after 2001 on the Atlantic coast and from 25% over the period 1989-1997 to 30% in 2004 on the gulf coast (Munyandorero et al. 2006). This increase in spawning stock is enough that recruitment failure for either the Atlantic coast or gulf coast stocks is highly unlikely. In fact, it appears that the stock could still maintain its production of recruits and provide more yield if fishing mortality were allowed to increase somewhat above 2004 levels (Muyandorero No).

Abundance by Month:  Murphy noted the monthly trends of commercial landings during 1986-1996 were highest in October through December on the Atlantic coast with an additional peak during March and April (1980).  On the Gulf coast, the highest catches were during November through March (Figure 10).

Abundance by Year:  Muller and Murphy estimated sheepshead population size(s) for each coast of Florida using a sequential population analysis (1979).  Between 1980 and 1992, the Atlantic coast population averaged approximately 4,000,000 sheepsheads, while the Gulf coast population averaged approximately 6,000,000 sheepsheads (1979).
	Standardized commercial catch rates on the Atlantic coast fluctuated without long-term trend during 1992–2007 (Fig. 3a Mud), in spite of a slight declining trend between 2001 and 2004. Commercial catch rates on the gulf coast show an inverse pattern to that seen on the Atlantic coast, with a steady increase since 1998, which peaked in 2003 (Fig. 3bMud). Total catch rates by recreational anglers have declined slightly from the early 1990s and there is no apparent trend in the catch rates from 2000-2007 on the Atlantic and gulf coasts (Figs 3c-d Mud).
	Indices of young-of-the-year (YOY) abundance for sheepshead varied erratically with peaks in 1996, 2000 and 2004 on the Atlantic coast (Fig. 4a). On the gulf coast the YOY index of abundance varied without trend but a strong year class was detected in 2000 (Fig 4b). The post-YOY abundance index for the Atlantic coast follows a cyclical pattern with lows in 2001 and 2006 (Fig. 4c). On the gulf coast the post-YOY index follows a pattern of high abundances in 1998 and 2003 followed by periods of decline (Fig. 4d).

[fig]

[/fig]

Population Abundance:  In 1996, an estimated 17.3 million sheepshead occurred in Florida (1980).  The Atlantic coast abundance peaked at 8.5 million sheepshead in 1990 and 1991 then dropped to 5.4 million by 1995.  The Gulf coast abundance peaked at 15.2 million sheepshead then dropped to 10.6 million in 1994 (1980).  Estimates of the total stock biomass of Florida have fluctuated around 7.1 million lbs. for the Atlantic coast and 9.5 million lbs. for the Gulf coast (1980).
	Murphy and MacDonald estimated abundance of sheepshead age 1 and older in Florida to be 21.6 million fish in 1999 (2006).  Estimates of abundance for both Florida coasts (Figure 11) did not show any trend during 1986-1999 although they were lower on the Atlantic coast (7.3 million fish) than on the Gulf coast (14.3 million fish.

nodes.title: Management Regulations
nodes.body:
Sheepshead harvest was not directly regulated in Florida until 1996 although various fishing restrictions enacted before then had indirectly impacted sheepshead fisheries. In 1996, the Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC) established a 12-inch fork length minimum-size limit for all harvesters and a 10-fish recreational bag limit. Commercial fishing was restricted to the use of hook-and-line, cast net, beach or haul-seine gear, with a 50-pound bycatch allowance for harvest by non-conforming gear. These regulations were modified in 1997 when the recreational bag limit was increased to 15 fish and commercial spearfishing was allowed (Citations).
	Florida recreational fishing regulations for sheepshead include a minimum size limit of 12 inches and a maximum bag limit of no more than 15 fish per person per day in or from state waters.  The harvest of sheepshead in or from Florida waters by or with the use of multiple hook(s) is prohibited.  Allowable recreational gear for the harvest of sheepshead includes beach or haul seine, cast net, hook and line gear, or by spearing.  Persons holding a valid saltwater products license may harvest sheepshead using other gear than recreationally allowed if sheepshead are incidental bycatch of other targeted species lawfully harvested, provided the number of sheepshead harvested do not exceed 50 lbs.
	Fishery management actions in the mid 1990s that led to a drop in total landings of sheepshead and a change in the size of fish landed included restrictions to the use of entangling nets, restricted species designation for sheepshead, the 12-inch FL minimum-size limit, a 10-fish bag limit (changed to 15 fish), and a 50 fish commercial possession limit. The associated decline in fishing mortality and shift in age-specific vulnerability to the fishery has been enough to allow for the increase in the spawning stock of sheepshead in Florida (citations?).

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall:  Sheepshead range from Nova Scotia, Massachusetts and the northern Gulf of Mexico to Rio de Janeiro (92 327 363 788 791).  Absent from the West Indies and the Bahamas (92 363 788 791).

Within Florida:  Common throughout Florida waters (664).  A.p. probatocephalus has 6 dark bars and is found on the East Coast and around the peninsula to Cedar Key, on the West Coast.  A.p. oviceps has 5 dark bands and is common in the northwestern, soft-bottomed Gulf of Mexico, east to Alligator Harbor, Florida (92).  A.p. oviceps is also associated with muddy substrates while A.p. probatocephalus occupies the eastern, hard bottomed, Gulf of Mexico (92 791).

By Stock:  Sheepshead are abundant throughout their geographic range, although it is believed current studies underestimate their abundance.  Few studies collect sheepshead with traditional sampling gears such as gill nets, seines, and trawls (546). Most gears are not selective for structure oriented fishes and sheepshead associate more commonly to structures such as oil and gas platforms, rocks, jetties, reefs, and piers. Boudreaux and Schenayder presented the results of a typical tow used in the finfish-monitoring program of the Louisiana Department of Wildlife and Fisheries (1985).  These results indicate gillnet and trammel nets are not effective for catching sheepshead unless set near shores and structures (1985).  Perret completed a comprehensive, coastwide study of Louisiana and attributed low catches to gear selectivity (546).  Fish (60 mm – 455 mm) were caught during all months of the year yet only 74 were sheepshead (40 caught by trawls and 34 caught by seines) (546).  Perret also noted local fishermen frequently made larger catches and concluded, “...this species (sheepshead) is much more common than is indicated by these results” (546).  Juneau attributed low catches of sheepshead (only 15) to gear selectivity in 2 years of trawl and seine sampling in the Vermilion-Atchafalaya bay complex (372).  Juneau also stated local fisherman caught more sheepshead using other gears (372).  The data from 10 years of Louisiana Department of Wildlife and Fisheries coastal gill net, trammel net, and seine samples exhibit similar trends (1992).  Although Reid caught no sheepshead in Cedar Key, Florida, while using a trawl, beam trawl, and various nets (cast, trammel, dip, push); he noted that 2 to 3 lb. sheepshead were caught in abundance by hook and line near a pier in the study area (581).  Sheepshead were rarely caught in over 400 shrimp trawls in Louisiana using a trawl mesh about 1.5 inches stretched (2002).  Gunter concluded that this gear excluded the shallower habitat and associated structures common to sheepshead (2002).

By Estuary:  Sheepshead are the second most abundant gamefish in the North River system which is adjacent to the Everglades estuary, (Florida and Whitewater bays) Florida (515).

Other Areas:  Sanchez Velasco found sheepshead larvae were most abundant during March in coastal areas off Terminos Lagoon, Campeche Bay, Mexico (1967).  Approximately 13% of all larvae collected were sheepshead (1967).  Sheepshead taken from Vermilion Bay in Louisiana were caught near shore with seine nets (188).  Lake Pontchartrain is a popular area for sheepshead fishermen in Louisiana (374 1952).  Kelley collected sheepshead throughout the Delta National Wildlife Refuge, South of Lake Pontchartrain, in the lower Mississippi River delta (374).

Mobility and Migration:

nodes.title: Life Mode
nodes.body:
Eggs: are buoyant and transparent; spawning typically occurs over the inter continental shelf.
Larvae: are pelagic.
Juveniles and adults: are dermersal omnivores, and prefer live, hard-bottomed areas.  Generally solitary or found in small groups associated with structure.  Does not school but may form feeding and spawning aggregations (47 363 634 1037 1988).

Spatial Strategy:  Sheepshead are resident estuarine species that migrate to offshore, coastal environments.  Kelley attributed the distribution of sheepshead in the Delta National Wildlife Refuge to food availability and depth because most of the specimens collected had consumed large amounts of Phragmites communis (roseau cane) and had no salinity preference (374).

Mobility:  Sheepshead are not a truly migratory species, they primarily move offshore and inshore (358).  Adults move to offshore waters in the spring and return to the bays after spawning.  Sheepshead remain in nearshore waters during warm seasons (summer) and move out of the estuaries during periods of low temperatures (winter) (47 188 255 358 374 1988).  Bryant completed a tagging study that revealed a maximum traveled distance of 109 km prior to the spawning season (1965).  Schwartz plotted sheepshead data using a length-weight equation and observed an absence of specimens between the sizes of 90 – 150 mm SL (1953).  Schwartz noted this absence coincides with juvenile and adult migration from seagrass habitats to pilings, jetties, and other hard substrates (1965).  Sheepshead collected by Kelley, also coincide with this offshore migration because the highest abundance of sheepshead occurred in July, yet none were caught after September (374).  Another comprehensive tagging study-called the $500,000 Florida Fishing Contest-took place in 1961.  The tagging took place throughout the entire state and was supported by private companies and included prizes for fishermen.  Most sheepshead were recaptured within 5 miles of the point of release (1968).  The longest distance traveled by a 430 mm (at release) sheepshead was more than 20 miles.  This individual traveled 25 miles in 19 days, covering an average distance of 1.32 miles per day (1968).  Although sheepshead appear to be highly mobile between estuarine habitats at certain life stages; they probably have low mobility within preferred habitats (pilings or seagrasses for example).

nodes.title: FOOD HABITS
nodes.body: Vaughan described sheepshead feeding behavior similar to other Sparids; an early dependence on zooplankton followed by a change to an omnivorous or vegetarian diet.  Their diets diversify as they mature and are largely controlled by the habitat type they occupy.  Younger sheepshead feed heavily on abundant inshore algae while adults migrate to live near bottom reefs offshore where benthic invertebrates dominate (532).  One study found an offshore diet to be more diversified (included 87 different species) than an inshore/estuarine diet (included 48 species) due to the increased availability and consumption of invertebrates (532).  Sheepshead diets are similar to that of whitebone and red porgies in that they all feed heavily on barnacles (1964).  Sheepshead, unlike these other Sparid species, are keystone predators in hard bottom habitats of the South Atlantic Bight (1964).  Their feeding ability is directly constrained by their oral jaw crushing force and morphology (1987).  Ogburn concluded algae might be an important source of nutrients for juvenile and adult sheepshead (1951 1980).

nodes.title: Food Items
nodes.body:
Benson summarized the diet of sheepshead as: larvae consuming primarily zooplankton, juveniles consuming zooplankton as well as polychaetes and chironomid larvae; large juveniles and adults consuming blue crabs, young oysters, clams, crustaceans and small fish (47).
Larvae:  Hildebrand and Cable found that ostracods were the primary food for fishes less than 30 mm (314).
Juveniles and Adults:  Juveniles and adults are omnivores, feeding on plant material (algae) as well as crustaceans, molluscs and small fishes (primarily young Atlantic croaker) (165 255 374 515 516 532 1988).  On offshore live bottom reefs in the South Atlantic Bight, sessile invertebrates dominated adult sheepshead diet with bryozoans being most important but including bivalves, echinoderms and acideans.  Barnacles and decapods were consumed in lesser amounts but foraminiferans, cnidarians, polychaetes, gastropods, and small arthropods were also eaten (634).  Within the grass beds of Florida Bay and Whitewater Bay, sheepshead (< 40 mm) fed on copepods, amphipods, chironomids, mysids and some algae.  At about 50 mm, juvenile sheepshead incorporate small molluscs as they migrate upstream (up the North River for example) to hard bottom habitat (515 1960).  Throughout ontogeny, sheepshead like most Sparids, depend increasingly on hard prey items (crabs, bivalves, gastropods and barnacles).  Larger fish consume increasingly larger and more robust bivalves such as the common mussel, the common oyster, and the Florida cardita (1987).  As this durophagic feeding behavior increases, so does the force generated by the adductor mandibulae complex (1987).  The oral jaw structure grows faster than overall size resulting in greater than proportional increases in crushing potential with additional size gains (1987).  Hernandez also determined that the realized jaw crushing force increases at the same rate as the potential jaw crushing force.  Sheepshead feeding ability is directly constrained by their oral jaw crushing force and morphology (1987).  Ogburn found juveniles (52-63 mm SL) at Fort Fisher Basin, North Carolina, consumed 69% by volume plant material (27% blue-green algae, 18% green algae, 14% brown algae, 6% diatoms and 4% red algae). The remaining 31% of the juvenile diet was invertebrates (primarily sponges) (1951).  Ogburn found adults (157-340 mm SL) at the Masonboro Inlet jetties took advantage of the lower intertidal and upper subtidal zones at high tide to forage (1951).  Adult sheepshead consumed 65% algae and 31% invertebrates.  Red algae comprised 42% of the total diet by volume in contrast to only 4% for juvenile sheepshead while green algae made up 21% by volume (1951).  Sixty-one percent of the invertebrates consumed by adults were mussels and only 2% were sponges (1951).  Ogburn’s documentation of the change in the invertebrate food items consumed by juveniles (sponges primarily) to adults (mussels primarily) emphasizes the role the morphology and development of the oral jaw structures play in the feeding ability of sheepshead (1951, 1987). Gunter concluded that sheepshead were largely herbivores because a majority of 18 sheepshead he analyzed in Texas waters had unusually long digestive tracks, and their stomachs contained large amounts of plant material (1992).  Ogburn found the relative lengths of the gut (RLG) of juvenile sheepshead to be 1.67 while small and large adults were 2.10 and 2.03, respectively (1951).  Fish with RLG values of 1.3 to 4.2 are generally considered omnivorous while RLG values below 2.4 are considered carnivorous (1951).  Ogburn notes that the smaller (and below 2.4) juvenile RLG value (1.67) may indicate a more carnivorous feeding habit than that of larger adults (2.10), although that was not supported by the study’s findings (1951).  In fact, a Tampa Bay study documented one 86mm (juvenile) sheepshead stomach completely contained filamentous green algae (664).  The dependence of sheepshead on plant material is unknown.  Although smaller fish frequently consume plant material, the plant material may have been incidental to foraging for small crustaceans on the plants, or vice versa (1992).

nodes.title: Habitat Type
nodes.body:
Egg:  Eggs are typically marine, in coastal waters of the inner continental shelf.  Larvae are known to be present in the Gulf of Mexico January through May, with peak abundance February through April (1982 1983 1988).
Larvae:  Larvae are pelagic as they move into estuaries, then become estuarine-dependent and associated with seagrasses.  The pelagic stage lasts until larvae are about 30 to 40 days old when metamorphosis into juveniles occurs.
Juvenile:  After metamorphosis, juveniles “settle out”, become substrate oriented, then move to nearshore reefs as they mature (634 1403 1988).
Adult:  Sheepshead and other pelagic reef fish are commonly associated with artificial reef habitats, particularly, petroleum platforms of the northern Gulf of Mexico (1970 2011).  Sonnier observed sheepshead associated with petroleum platforms off Louisiana (between 91 30 W and 93 W) in water depths of 18-55 meters (2011).  Stanley and Wilson have coupled two fisheries-independent monitoring techniques, dual-beam hydroacoustics and visual point count surveys, to provide estimates of fish assemblages associated with petroleum platforms.  A 15 month monitoring project of the West Cameron 352 petroleum platform (80 km south of Louisiana in 20 m of water) revealed sheepshead accounted for approximately 10% of the total fish surveyed (average = 12,473 total fish) and sheepshead were observed on every visual survey (1970).  The large monthly variation observed in size distribution and density of sheepshead could be attributed to emigration, immigration and possible recruitment. These results support the open nonequilibrial system hypothesis describing fish abundance on reef habitats (1970).  The hydroacoustics also estimated the first quantified measurement of the near-field area of influence surrounding an artificial reef; 16 m on either side of the platform based on continuous fish densities from 2 to 72 m (1970).

nodes.title: Substrate
nodes.body:
Egg:  Eggs are not associated with particular substrate(s) because they are strictly marine.
Larvae:  Larvae are pelagic and no information was found on substrate associations.
Juvenile:  Juveniles are usually associated with seagrass beds until they are around 50 mm then they move into the more typical adult habitats (188 373 515 1037 1050 1960).
Adult:  Adults are demersal occurring nearshore around oyster beds, shallow, muddy or rocky bottoms, Spartina marshes, piers, rocks, and jetties (47 515 848 1037 1960 1988).  Adults also can be found in bare sand surf zones feeding on infaunal bivalves and crustaceans (1984 1988).  A 285-mm sheepshead was collected off a mud bottom in an oil field of Vermilion Bay, Louisiana that contained several artificial structures that likely serve as a preferential habitat (188).  Over 4,000 petroleum platforms exist in the northern Gulf of Mexico, providing an additional 12 km2 of natural hard substrate to the approximately 2600 km2 of natural hard bottom (1970 2011). It is largely accepted that rock reefs enhance fish populations whether or not kelp (Macrocystis pyrifera) is present (1976).  Putt assessed the fish species distribution in various hard bottom areas of the northwestern Gulf of Mexico.  Sheepshead were most abundant in the hard substrate habitats less than 35 meters deep with sheer rock outcrops rising 3 meters from the seafloor (1969).

nodes.title: Submerged Vegetation
nodes.body:
Egg:  No data available.
Larvae:  Need information.
Juvenile:  Juvenile sheepsheads are most abundant in grass flats or over mud bottoms (47 358 515 664 1960).
Adult:   similar affinity to seagrasses as juveniles.

nodes.title: Depth Distribution
nodes.body:
Egg:  No data available.
Larvae:  Need information.
Juvenile:  Need information although below study includes juveniles.
Adult:  Lindquist observed a sheepshead depth preference at the north jetty of Wrightsville Beach, North Carolina.  A majority of the individuals were observed at the shallower (2 m vs. 4 m) depth.  This behavior is attributed to preferred food availability at the different depths.  Stomach content analysis confirmed the sheepshead were feeding on algae and mussels that are more abundant on the littoral rock surfaces in the upper water stratum (1975).

nodes.title: Temperature
nodes.body:
Egg:  No data available.
Larvae:  Need information.
Juvenile:  Juveniles have been collected in temperatures ranging from 8.0 C to 29.6 C (358 561 1985).
Adult:  Adults have been collected in temperatures from 5.0 C to 35.1 C (116 546 603 709).  A comprehensive study of the Biloxi marsh in Louisiana observed catch rates of sheepshead declined when waters dropped below 11 C or when waters reached 35 C (220).  Seventy-one sheepshead were collected during an extensive inventory of the Lake Pontchartrain-Lake Maurepas estuary, in Louisiana, and the greatest catch probability occurred between 30 to 35 C (709).  No information on lethal upper and lower thermal limits for larvae, juveniles, or adults has been found in the literature.

nodes.title: Salinity
nodes.body:
Sheepshead are euryhaline (261), found in waters with salinity’s from 0 - 45 ppt (47 188 193 372 358 374 546 548 651 709 1051 1988).
Egg:  No data available.
Larvae:  Larvae have been collected from 5.0 - 24.9 ppt (116).
Juvenile:  Need information.
Adult:  Adults range in salinity’s from 0.4 - 43.8 ppt (261 515 709 790 1051).  Tarver and Savoie found the greatest catch probability for sheepshead in Louisiana occurred at a salinity range of 5.0 to 9.9 ppt (709). Sheepshead(s) were also found in the Fish Bowl, the largest of the Homosassa Springs, Florida.  Salinity was 570 parts chloride per million and the fish were not observed in other springs, either in the Weekiwachee or the Chassahowitska rivers (1051).  Fontenot and Rogillio compared sheepshead monthly catch rates from the Biloxi marsh, Louisiana to the salinity ranges sampled.  During some months, peak catches occurred at the low (0-4 ppt) and high (>=20 ppt) extremes of salinities sampled, while other months showed little variation in catches across salinities (220).  The authors concluded from this that the normal changes in salinity in the Biloxi marsh did not affect the movement of the sheepshead to and from the lagoon and lake areas (220).

nodes.title: Dissolved Oxygen
nodes.body:
Egg:  No data available.
Larvae:  Need information.
Juvenile:  Need information.
Adult:  Minimum dissolved oxygen tolerance is not known for this species but Adkins and Bowman attributed sheepshead deaths in semiopen and closed canals of Louisiana to oxygen depletion; which resulted from aerobic (and anaerobic) organic decomposition (4).

Turbidity:  A Wrightsville Beach, North Carolina study of fish utilization patterns on various jetties documented sheepshead in the Masonboro Inlet jetty.  During maximum flood or ebb, tidal flow velocity reaches 4 km per hour resulting in considerable turbidity (1975).  Sheepshead studied in Biloxi marsh, Louisiana were sampled at stations with turbidity commonly less than 25 and seldomly greater than 50 (units not reported) (220).

PH:  Sheepshead studied in Biloxi marsh, Louisiana were found in waters with an average pH of 8 (220).

Light/Photoperiod:  Dugas sampled fish in Vermilion Bay, Louisiana over multiple 24 hour (night and day) periods and captured ten sheepshead (190).  In July 1968, the author collected seven sheepshead at night indicating sheepshead may have significant activity during non-daylight hours (190).

Currents/Tides: Sheepshead collected in one study had 8% flood tide and 0.4% ebb (603).  The maximum vertical tide range at the Masonboro Inlet jetty where sheepshead have been studied is 1.8 m (1975).  The tidal flow velocity can reach 4 km per hour during maximum tidal flows (1975).  Fontenot and Rogillio found the most successful catches of sheepshead occurred during the prevailing high-falling or prevailing high-rising tidal conditions of the Biloxi marsh, Louisiana (220).

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body:
Reproductive Periodicity:  Render and Wilson estimated spawning frequency from once per day to once every 20 days (1958).  Fontenot and Rogillio analyzed sheepshead gonads for maturity (ripeness) and found the spawning period in the Biloxi marsh to extend from February through May, with a minor period from October through December (220).  Spawning was observed during temperature range 16 C to 30 C with the greatest amount occurring during the 21 C to 25 C range (220).

Domain:  Young-of-the-year enter the North River, (from the Everglades estuary) Florida in June continuing until late fall (515).  Odum noted sheepshead is the second most abundant game fish of the North River system because of the abundance of suitable habitat (exposed rocky bottom) and preferred prey items (hydroids and crustaceans).  Springer and Woodburn found young-of-the-year in the Tampa Bay area from June through October (664).

Fertilization: Sheepshead have separate male and female sexes (gonochoristic), and are oviparous, broadcast spawners with pelagic eggs (363).  Fertilization is external, by broadcast of milt and roe into the water column.

Spawning Strategy:  Spawning probably occurs offshore (664), during the spring; late February through late April (116 314 664 1958).  Peak spawning occurs during the months of March and April (1950).  Spawning may occur earlier in the southern Indian River Lagoon as <10-mm SL specimens were collected in January at Ft. Pierce and Sebastian Inlets (1271).  Although some literature suggests spawning may occur within estuaries, the only sheepshead observed having post-ovulatory follicles in advanced stages of maturity have been collected from offshore waters (1958 1981).

Parental Care:  No data available.

Seasonal Energetics:  No data available.

Maturation:  Sheepshead apparently begin to mature at age 2 (1954 1958 FWC-FMRI unpublished data 1980 1981).  However, fewer mature females occur in this and subsequent age classes in Florida and Georgia than in Louisiana.  Render and Wilson collected sheepshead in Louisiana that were mature by age 2; all males over age 3 and all females over age 4 in the study were mature (1958). Music and Pafford found in Georgia that the smallest female with developing ovaries was age 3 (282 mm TL) and the smallest male was age 4 (393 mm TL) (1981).   In Tampa Bay, Florida, nearly all males were mature by age 1; however, only 2% of females were mature at age 1, 15% at age 2, and 60% at age 3 (FWC-FWRI unpublished data 1980).

The Sparidae family exhibits hermaphroditism more complexly than other fishes.  Sparid species (following examples I have not accurately confirmed yet, Acanthopagrus australis  pagellus acarne  --  Chrysophrys major Pagellus erythrinus – Acanthopagrus cuvieri Diplodus annularis) exhibit protandry and protogyny hermaphroditism as well as rudimentary hermaphroditism in which they develop into functional gonochorists.  Young rudimentary hermaphrodites possess an intersexual gonad but mature as either male or female fish with no sex reversal, hence the term functional or late gonochorists (1972).  Render and Wilson concur with Buxton and Garratt that the bipotentiality of Sparids including Archosargus probatocephalus is a preadaptation for the development of hermaphroditism in species in which reproductive success is related to size (1972, 2003).

Fecundity: Tucker and Barbera obtained 15,000 eggs from strip spawning a 398 g running ripe female (1954).  Fecundity appears to vary between fish from the inshore area, and older, larger fish caught offshore (1958).  Fish caught offshore had an average fecundity of 87,000 eggs/batch and ranged from 14,000 to 250,000 eggs/batch.  The average fecundity of fish from inshore areas was 11,000 eggs/batch, and ranged 1,100 to 40,000 eggs/batch (1958).  The significant difference in batch size from sheepshead collected nearshore and offshore was not understood due to the low sample size of females (10 specimens) with hydrated eggs (1958). Given uncertainties of total seasonal fecundity and the large variation of batch fecundities, an estimate of the relationship between length and total fecundity would be highly variable (1958).  Spawning frequency was uncertain yet speculated to be from 1 to 20 days (1958).    Music and Pafford found sheepshead 428-591 mm TL and 4-14 years old, ranged from 296,000 to 963,000 eggs (mean = 604,559 eggs) (1981).

nodes.title: Development
nodes.body:
Egg:	Eggs are buoyant and hatching occurs in about 40 hours at 24  25 C (47 363).  Tucker observed eggs with a mean diameter of 0.82 mm (0.80 to 0.85 mm) and a single oil globule hatched in 28 hrs at 23 C (1956).
Larvae: Mook completed a detailed description (including drawings) of larval development (484).  Larvae are about 2.0 mm when they hatch and by 5 mm they have absorbed the yolk sac.  The oil droplet starts decreasing at 3 mm and disappears at 7 mm.  The median fins form in the following order: caudal, anal, and dorsal.  The caudal fin is apparent at 3 mm and well developed by 4 mm (484).  The anal fin appears at 4 mm and by 6 mm is well developed including all three spines, and the eleven lepidotrichia found in the adult (484).  The pectoral fins are the first paired fins to develop, appearing at 2mm and becoming well developed at 8 mm.  Pelvic fins are also well developed by 8 mm, first appearing at 6.5 mm (484).    Larvae range from 525 mm and the transition to the juvenile stage begins at about 12 mm (484).  Pigmentation in yolk-sac larvae is limited to one small melanophore at the angle of the jaws and three melanophores along the ventral side of the body posterior to the vent.  Some pre-larvae may have one or two small melanophores on the yolk-sac yet most melanophores disappear by 6 mm (358 484).  No further pigmentation is present on larvae after this stage until they begin to assume their adult pigmentation (484).  Larval sheepshead greater than 4.5 mm SL have about 24 well-developed and distinguishable myomeres (484).  Larval sheepshead jaw elements ossify quickly and are all present by 3 mm (484).  By 4.5 mm, thirteen premaxillary and six dentary teeth are present (484).  At 8 mm, narrow, sharp teeth line the jaws and by 9 mm, incisors first appear on the anterior end of the jaw.  The incisors dominate the anterior end of the jaw by 15 mm and the posterior teeth have thickened to form adult molars resulting in the typical sparid dentition described by Soshichi (484).  These first teeth look more like those of an unspecialized carnivore rather than the typical sparid teeth and are suspected to contain primitive features of early sheepshead ancestors’ (484).  Mook was unable to observe these primitive jaw features in larvae because some of the small bones decalcified due to storage in formalin (484).
Juvenile:  Validated daily growth rings place the duration of pelagic larvae (from hatch to settlement) between 30 and 40 days, at a length of approximately 8 mm SL (1952).  Parsons and Peters found that this might be the beginning of the juvenile stage (1403) while Mook estimates it to occur at about 12 mm (484).
Adult:  Most adult skull elements and the characteristic Sparid dentition are formed by 8 mm (484).  Adult coloration begins at the caudal end at about 7 mm and gradually extends forward; bars are distinguishable by 11 mm (484).  Tucker noted live larvae raised in captivity had five distinct vertical bands 25 hours after hatching (1971).  As sheepshead grow, the pigmentation patterns darken and stabilize, and by 25-30 mm, the adult pattern forms (363, 484).   Growth is rapid up to 6 to 8 years of age, after which it levels off (1950).  Reported age at maturity is 2-4 years (1957) although the minimum size at sexual maturity is unknown (363).  Individuals may live over 20 years of age (1950) and can grow up to 730 mm TL (596 mm SL) (1953).

nodes.title: Length Range
nodes.body:
Egg:  Need information.
Larvae:  Need information.
Juvenile:  Need information.
Adult:  The largest sheepshead recorded is from Louisiana at 730 mm TL and weighed about 20 lbs (1953).  Sheepshead caught off North Carolina and Texas have been recorded at approximately 723 mm TL (1952, 1953).  Schwartz maintains that 730 mm TL is the largest verifiable size attainable for sheepshead and other references in the literature should be amended (1953).

Length Conversions:  MacDonald calculated relations among total, standard, and fork length from unpublished data collected by the Florida Marine Research Institute (1980).

 	mm FL = 0.9084 (mm TL) + 1.20	n = 1469	r^2 = 0.994
 	mm SL = 0.8116 (mm TL) – 5.70	n = 1710	r^2 = 0.987
 	mm TL = 1.0947 (mm FL) + 0.52 	n = 1469	r^2 = 0.994
 	mm SL = 0.8933 (mm FL) – 6.78	n = 1469	r^2 = 0.989
 	mm FL = 1.1065 (mm SL) + 10.89 	n = 1469	r^2 = 0.989
 	mm TL = 1.1038 (mm SL) + 11.10	n = 1710	r^2 = 0.987
[/eq]
Schwartz published equations for predicting standard length from total length (1953).
[eq]
 	SL (mm) = 0.817 (mm TL) for fish larger than 100 mm SL
 				and
 	SL (mm) = 0.780 (mm TL) for fish smaller than 100 mm SL
[/eq].

Weight-Length Relationship:  Beckman noted otolith weight is a better age estimator than annulus deposition because otolith growth is continuous and independent of fish growth at intermediate ages.  Although annulus formation occurred during the spawning period (March –April) it is not a result of spawning because it occurred during the same period in mature and immature sheepshead (1950).  Sheepshead age is not a reliable predictor of weight or length (1950).  Florida specific weight/length relationships were calculated (1980) using pooled, sex-combined data resulting in differences between the Atlantic and Gulf coast stocks (standard errors in parentheses).
[eq]
Atlantic:  Weight (g) = 3.315E-05 (mm FL) 2.963
						  (6.0E-06)                 (0.03214)
Gulf:       Weight (g) = 4.816E-05 (mm FL) 2.885
						   (5.5E-06)                (0.01951)

[/eq]
Length at Age:  The sagitta is the largest otolith in sheepshead and is laterally compressed with an oval shape and a pointed rostrum.  The most accurate age estimates of individual sheepshead are sagitta counts (one annulus forms per year) of annuli deposited on the medial surface, ventral to the sulcus (1950).  Music and Pafford calculated a least-square regression on the relationship between fish length and scale radius (1981).  The length/age relationship (cm) is:
[eq]
Age =  0.000043 L ^(1.953)		n = 118, r ^2= 0.86
[/eq]
Murphy determined that sheepsheads up to age 6 were slightly larger on the Florida Atlantic coast than those on the Florida Gulf coast.  Afterwards, Gulf coast sheepsheads were larger at age (1980).  On average, sheepsheads reach about 260 mm FL between ages 1 and 2, 305 mm FL between ages 2 and 3, and 350 mm FL between ages 3 and 4 (1980).

Longevity:  Sheepshead probably live more than 20 years given the Louisiana gamefish record is 9.6 kg (Louisiana Outdoor Writers Assoc. 1987).  The oldest sheepshead based on otolith and scale readings was 14 years old from a sample of 105 sheepshead from Georgia (1981).  Maximum ages of Florida Sheepshead are apparently 11 years for males and 14 years for females (1980).  Beckman lists other Sparids that have greater longevity than Sheepshead, including Cymatoceps nasutus (45yrs) and Chrysophrys auratus (60yrs) (1950).

nodes.title: Growth Equations
nodes.body:
Music and Pafford determined a length/weight relationship for 118 sheepshead (101 – 591 mm TL and 21 – 4,297 g) collected off Georgia (1981).
[eq]
log (Wt) = 2.885 log (TL) – 4.412	r =0.9707
[/eq]

Schwartz calculated another length/weight relationship (1953) for North Carolina Sheepshead on 282 fish (9-591 mm SL and 0.042 – 8370 g) as follows:
[eq]
log (Wt) = 3.0446 log (SL) - 4.5287	   r = 0.9929
[/eq]
Beckman weighed and measured 784 specimens collected in the Mississippi River delta area (1950) and calculated a length/weight regression as follows:
[eq]
Wt = 5.46 x 10^-5 FL^ 2.86 	 r ^2 = 0.923
[/eq]
Additional growth curves separating sexes produced significantly better fit by length and weight compared to curves that combined sexes.  Music and Pafford calculated (1981) the following length/weight regression (cm TL):
[eq]
Wt = 0.000039 TL^ 2.885	r ^2 = 0.97
[/eq]
Beckman growth curves show sheepshead grow rapidly to an asymptotic size at age 6-8.  The growth coefficient, K, for sheepsheads is relatively larger than other Sparids at 0.42 (1950).  Murphy and MacDonald developed von Bertalanffy growth curves for males and female sheepshead caught in Tampa Bay (2006). nodes.title: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
nodes.body:
Competition:  Need information.

Predation: Sheepshead predation of competitively superior benthic invertebrates may be important in controlling the structure of sessile invertebrate and motile epifauna communities’ (634).  Although adult sheepshead consume a diversity of prey, they likely exhibit some caution/avoidance of polychaetes known to have effective anti-predation responses such as    Phyllodoce mucosa (a predatory worm) (1959).  Little information exists regarding the predation of sheepshead life stages, but it likely that larvae and juveniles could be food sources for predatory fishes (1988).

Parasites/Diseases:  Sheepshead are hosts of ciliates, nematodes, trematodes, and isopods; none of which are known to endanger populations of the species (358).  Some pathogenic parasites of sheepshead include the trematodes, Multitestis rotundus, Cotylogaster basiri, and Lepocreadium archosargi; the nematodes, Hysterothylacium reliquens (type MA) and Thynnascaris reliquens sp. n. (532, 1992, 1995, 1997, 1999, 2006, 2007, 2013).   Sogandares-Bernal and Hutton discovered 1 in 3 sheepshead had intestine infections of Multitestis rotundus in Bayboro Harbor, Tampa Bay, Florida (1993). Deardorff and Overstreet described type MA of Hysterothylacium reliquens in sheepshead and other fish of the Gulf of Mexico, noting it is most commonly found in fish mesenteries (1999).  Norris and Overstreet found Thynnascaris reliquens sp. n. in the stomachs and intestines of sheepshead from the Mississippi sound (1995).   Fifteen out of twenty-three mature males and fifteen out of twenty-four gravid females were infected by the nematode, Thynnascaris reliquens sp. n. (1995).  Overstreet noted the dinoflagellate, Amyloodinium ocellatum and the isopod, Lironeca ovalis also parasitize sheepshead (2004).  Many fresh and saltwater fish species of Mississippi, including sheepshead, suffer from red sore disease (1996).   Red sore disease is caused by the ciliate, Epistylis sp. and common effects include severe hemorrhaging, lesions and subsequent bacterial infections (1996).  Fish mortalities are attributed to these secondary bacterial infections (1996).  The most common bacterium associated with red sore disease is Aeromonas hydrophilia (1996).  Once a colony of Epistylis sp. becomes well established, Aeromonas hydrophilia invades and can be found in the lesions and organs of the infected fish (1996).  The high incidence of red sore disease in Escatawpa estuary, Mississippi, resulted in considerably reduced fish catches.  Epistylis sp. infestations are associated with polluted and organic rich estuaries that are not rapidly flushed, such as the Escatawpa estuary (1996).  Epistylis sp. infests a variety of fishes but can also grow on organic debris and hard substrates (1996).  Overstreet also reported a unique parasitic relationship in sheepshead (533).  Myxosporidians generally parasitize cold blooded vertebrates; however, one species (Fabespora vermicola) infects a fluke that occurs in the intestines of sheepshead (1992, 2004).    Multi-species fish kills including sheepshead were observed in the Indian River, Florida from mid September to mid October 1996 in association with an observed algal bloom.  The dinoflagellate, Gymnodinium pulchellum was verified in water samples taken in an 83 km range of the Indian River, corresponding to the area of the observed bloom and the fish kills (1990, 1998).  Cell counts ranged from 6.67 x 10^2 to 19.7 x 10^6 cells/L (1990).  Subsequent fish bioassays did not confirm the toxicity of Gymnodinium pulchellum however, the presence of Gymnodinium pulchellum at two separate fish kills in 1990 and 1996, in the same location, suggest that this dinoflagellate species is ichthyotoxic (1990).  The discovery of Gymnodinium pulchellum increases the number of potentially toxic marine and estuarine dinoflagellate species in Florida to 25 (1990).

Oil Spills:  No data available.

Contamination:  No data available.

Eutrophication:  No data available.

Pollutant Toxicity:  Sheepshead are apparently more susceptible to the acute lethal toxicity of copper than the latent toxicity (72 hour TLm = 2.19 ppm Cu/I).  Initial hyperactivity follows 72 hour static copper exposure (0.1, 0.2, or 0.4 ppm Cu/I) resulting in faster, more erratic swimming behavior (1974 1986).  Sheepshead’s natural preference for smaller turns also increased (1974).  One week following exposure, sheepshead exhibited extreme hypoactivity, and this latent toxicity is presumably the result of the physiological stress produced by the initial hyperactivity, and the accumulated physiological damage due to Copper exposure (1974).  Cardeilhac exposed 4 sheepshead (665 – 980 g) to toxic concentrations of copper (8.5 ppm) in seawater (1977).  The authors identified five stages of intoxication: lethargy (minimal avoidance of capture), indifference (no avoidance of capture), incoordination (disoriented movement), moribundity (complete loss of posture), and death (1977). These stages of intoxication following acute copper poisoning are believed to be the result of potassium intoxication caused by cell damage and osmoregulatory failure (1977).  It has been suggested that initial hyperactivity after acutely sublethal exposure to heavy metals may be an “advantageous” behavioral response by increasing the chance the fish will leave the polluted area (1977, 2009).  However, sheepsheads’ erratic response and increased preference for shorter turns will more than likely not improve an individual’s ability to vacate a polluted area (1974).  Steele compared the behavioral and acute toxicity of sheepshead to pinfish and Atlantic croaker, and found sheepshead was the most susceptible species (1986).  Its 96 h TLm was 1.14 ppm of copper ion (1986).  The acute toxicity results did not distinguish between behaviorally less sensitive species (1986).

Entrainment/Impingement:  No data available.

Perturbations:  No data available.

Climate:  No data available.

Other:  Juvenile and adult sheepshead caught off Morehead city, North Carolina were raised in captivity to observe algae growth patterns.  Algae only grew on broken or damaged fin, spine, or scale surfaces.  Enteromorpha intestinalis grew densely and longest (up to 150 mm) during the hottest month of the year, July.  The sheepshead made no attempts to remove the algae growths (1973).    Sheepshead are associated with the nearly 4,000 oil and gas platforms (as of 1993) of the Gulf of Mexico (1966).  Owners of these artificial structures are required by federal regulations to remove closed structures within one year.  The most economical means of removal involves underwater explosives and significantly threatens marine life.  The Mineral and Mining Service (MMS) requires owners to obtain a permit prior to using explosives in federal waters (coastal waters of the Gulf of Mexico also require state permits).  The presence of 5 species of threatened or endangered sea turtles in the Gulf of Mexico requires an incidental take statement as part of the MMS permit.  Mandated by the Endangered Species Act, the National Marine Fisheries Service began monitoring the effects of the explosive removals on sea turtles and other marine life in 1987.  Over 63,000 total fish kills occurred between July and October in 30-45 meters of water. Sheepshead was the third most abundant fish species killed by explosive platform removals (1966).  No sea turtle deaths were reported in 1993 from explosive platform removals (1966).  Sheepshead apparently depend on these structures for habitat shelter, and food items (increased area for barnacles).  The removal of these oil and gas platforms may reduce the forage habitat of sheepshead and possibly decrease their population(s) (1992).  Sonnier noted the prevalence of these artificial sheepshead habitats off Louisiana (1962).  He states approximately 3,000 platforms exist off Louisiana and that it is nearly impossible to go anywhere offshore and within 140 km of the coastline, and not be in sight of several platforms (1962).
